svg.aria-label: Diagram: the two Amazon Bedrock capacity products and the different way each one fails. On the left, on-demand inference, where you are throttled by a tokens-per-minute quota set at the model level. A request deducts its total input tokens plus its max_tokens value at the start, before the model generates anything, and the request is throttled if that sum exceeds the quota. When the response is finished the deduction is adjusted to input tokens plus cache write tokens plus output tokens multiplied by a burndown rate, and cached read tokens are not counted toward the quota at all. The burndown rate is fifteen times for Claude 4.8 output tokens, ten times for Claude Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5, Opus 5 and Fable 5.1, five times for Anthropic models version 4.7 and below, and one to one for all other models, while billing remains one to one throughout, so quota and cost are consumed at different rates. A panel gives AWS's own worked example, where a request of one thousand input tokens generating one hundred output tokens on Claude Sonnet 4 depletes one thousand five hundred tokens of quota but is billed for one thousand one hundred. On the right, Provisioned Throughput, bought in model units where each unit delivers a set number of input tokens per minute and output tokens per minute, with the note that the actual figure per model unit and its price are not published and require contacting an AWS account manager. Its commitment terms are no commitment, deletable at any time, one month, and six months, where a committed purchase cannot be deleted before the term completes. A closing panel records that the commitment renews automatically at the end of each term, that cancelling auto renew still charges the full fee for the current term whether or not inference runs, that auto renew cannot be re-enabled once cancelled, and that no further modifications are possible for the remainder of the term.
svg.title: Two products, two failure modes: quota you can measure, commitment you cannot exit
svg.text: Quota and cost are both counted in tokens, and spent at different rates
Budgeting from the price list sizes the bill correctly and says nothing about when you get throttled.
On-demand — throttled by a tokens-per-minute quota
At the start of the request, before anything is generated:
total input tokens + max_tokens — throttled if this exceeds the quota
At the end, adjusted to what was actually used:
input + cache write + (output x burndown rate)
Burndown rate, output tokens only:
15x Claude 4.8 · 10x Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5, Opus 5, Fable 5.1 · 5x Anthropic 4.7 and below
1:1 all other models · cache reads are not counted toward the quota at all
Billing stays 1:1 throughout. Only the quota multiplies.
AWS's example: 1,000 in + 100 out on Sonnet 4 → 1,500 quota depleted, 1,100 billed.
Provisioned Throughput — a reservation, billed hourly
Bought in Model Units. One MU delivers a set number of
input tokens per minute and output tokens per minute
— the actual figures are not published.
“contact your AWS account manager” for MU size and price
Commitment terms:
No commitment — delete at any time
1 month · 6 months — cannot be deleted before the term ends
Custom models cannot be invoked without one.
Billing continues until you delete it.
A generation-heavy request on a 15x model: 1,000 in, 1,000 out
quota burned 1,000 + (1,000 x 15) = 16,000 · tokens billed 2,000 · eight times as much quota as cost
The commitment is a one-way door, and so is the exit from it
1. A committed Provisioned Throughput cannot be deleted before its term completes.
2. It renews automatically at the end of each term, keeping the same configuration.
3. Cancelling auto renew still charges the full fee for the current term, whether or not you run inference.
4. After cancelling, no further modifications are possible — and auto renew cannot be re-enabled.
Every step is documented behaviour. None of it is an error, and none of it is reversible.
Two endpoints, bedrock-runtime and bedrock-mantle, hold separate quotas for the same model. Burndown applies only to runtime.
Compute the quota cost of your own traffic from CloudWatch first. The on-demand crossover cannot be derived from public figures.
